text: By Tuesday night, Jaeha is back at that pier, looking down through Nib's eyes.
Nib crouches on a flange barely wider than his feet, the black river far below.
On the rooftop, Jaeha narrates with his eyes shut, as a foreman counts cash into five hands.
Five numbers on the clipboard, not a single name. If one goes missing, it's just a gap in a column.
Bomi is a step ahead of him. They're hiring.
The ad is written for people nobody will look for. Next shift: Thursday night.
The truck is stacked high with glowing crates. Since Saturday's stream, Kanghan is hurrying.
Then a guard swings his torch straight up at the girders.
Nib flattens on the steel. A fat pigeon lands on his head, and the guard blames the birds.
Jaeha bites back a laugh and passes on Nib's opinion of the pigeon.
Wednesday evening, the whole team crams into the rooftop room. Jaeha means to join Thursday's crew.
Choi is against it from the first word. Two million people just saw Jaeha's face.
Jaeha has thought of that. Behind a dark visor, Saturday's hero is just another number.
Choi jerks a thumb at Borro's face in the window. Some husks don't fit under a visor.
So only Jaeha uses the door. Nib goes over the top, Borro walks the riverbed, and Lyra swims in underwater.
Borro likes it down there. Lyra takes the doubt as an insult to her whole people.
Yerin asks what everyone's thinking. Jaeha counts off the backup: Choi's van, Bomi on watch, and her bandages.
Choi rubs his eyes and complains, but the complaint comes with a time and a parking spot.
Jaeha misses it and keeps arguing. Hating a plan, Choi says, isn't refusing it.
Seoa says nothing at all.
Then she grabs his sleeve. She doesn't fight the plan. She books him for Friday dinner and makes him swear.
So he does, with a pinky promise and a thumb stamp.
On the sill, Nib watches the bridge. He's the only one who's been there.
Thursday, ten minutes to the shift. Five people in grey coveralls wait by a van. One is Jaeha.
Foreman Gu hands out tabards and masks without looking at a face. Names are the first thing to go.
Jaeha's tabard says four.
Number one, Uncle Pyo, sixty-three, wears a knee brace. He spots a first-timer and shares two rules that kept him alive.
He has done this since the gates first opened. His knees have kept a longer count.
Number two, Dami, shows him her daughter's photo. Dami is risking her life for a school bag.
And the Jang brothers, Woo and Ho, are saving for a chicken shop, if they ever agree on its name.
Jaeha watches them, very still. He knows these people. He was these people.
A whistle, and five faces vanish behind smoky visors.
Single file, they walk toward the glowing slit under pier seven, each behind a plain white husk.
Under the river, Borro walks the bottom like a moving hill, and Lyra glides beside him, at home.
Nib slides down a cable from the bridge and lands without a sound, right above a guard.
Then Jaeha steps into the slit, into the gate where hyung died, and the light swallows him.
Inside: a vast canyon in violet twilight, steel walkways bolted down its walls, and pipes as thick as trucks humming into the dark.
Everyone stares straight down, except Pyo, who watches his boots and sighs.
Only Jaeha sees the three threads of light: Nib above, Borro and Lyra below, all within range.
The foreman sends them down with the oldest rule in the trade, and a price per trap.
A husk steps on a carved stone plate, and a stone spike smashes it into the abyss.
The foreman doesn't even look up. One tick, ten thousand won, and on they go.
A window only Jaeha sees confirms his notebook: unregistered, open four years, and the boss alive.
Jaeha knows that number without counting. It's exactly how long hyung has been gone.
Jaeha pretends to tie a boot and reads the old carved plates. Their spirals give the armed ones away: they open left.
Pyo is about to step past his husk, bad knee first, onto an armed one. Jaeha warns him quietly.
Pyo's husk takes the step instead, and a stone blade scythes its legs off at knee height.
Pyo stares. Ten years in gates, and a first-nighter just saved his knee. Jaeha calls it luck.
The foreman notices. Numbers aren't supposed to be clever.
Down they go. Nib keeps pace along the pipes, and far below, two shapes move in the river.
Ho feels a slow pulse through his glove, as if the canyon were alive. Woo blames the pipes.
At the first landing stands an engineers' cabin, bolted to the rock.
Then a radio call ruins the foreman's night: Kanghan's heir is coming down, and no one can turn her away.
He rounds on the crew, baton crackling. When she comes, they're to be what Kanghan thinks they are: husks.
Ho asks who that is. Woo's answer is bitter: someone who never had to work like them.
Then, from above: a sharp clack, in perfect rhythm.
Forty polished white husks march down two by two, every foot landing at once.
The crew flatten against the rock and the foreman bows. Only number four stays put, counting steps.
A white heeled boot steps onto the steel.
The column parts, and down the middle walks the woman in white from the guild hall, as if the abyss isn't there.
She looks the row over like stock on a shelf: that line on her tablet, in the flesh.
Her reflection sits small in his visor. In the gate Kanghan pretends isn't here: Kanghan's own heir.
Her baton points into the dark, and forty faces turn with it. She picks who goes first: the one who didn't flinch.
Jaeha bows like a waiter and gives her the line he gave Mok: it's a very brave husk.
Far below, one throb of violet light runs down the pipes and fades. Maybe Ho wasn't being weird.
